architecture.title: From a BF16 checkpoint to a fast NVFP4 server — quantize once, then speculate at serve time
architecture.caption: Model Optimizer runs inside NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM container on the Spark. It calibrates on sample text, rewrites the weights as NVFP4 (4-bit E2M1 values + one FP8 scale per 16), and exports a Hugging Face checkpoint with hf_quant_config.json. trtllm-serve loads it on :8355 (the course port). Speculative decoding is a serve-time option in the same engine: a draft (an EAGLE-3 head or a small FP4 model) proposes tokens and the target checks them in one pass.

sequence.title: One speculative decoding step (k = 4 drafted tokens)
sequence.caption: The draft proposes 4 tokens cheaply, one after another. The target scores all of them in ONE forward pass, which costs about the same as a normal decode step because decode is memory-bound (lab 04, Step 1). Tokens are accepted left to right until the first disagreement; the target then adds its own token. So each step yields between 1 and k+1 tokens, and the output is what the target would have produced anyway.

charts.title: Quantization error on 65,536 weight-like numbers (higher is better)
charts.caption: From lab 01 (pure Python, seeded, so the same on every machine). Bits per value including scales: 8 · 4.5 · 4.25 · 4.125 · 4. NVFP4's 16-value FP8-scaled blocks keep the error flat when outliers appear; formats with bigger blocks or coarser scales lose accuracy. This is layer-level error, not model accuracy.

charts.title: Expected tokens per target pass vs draft length
charts.caption: E = (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α), from lab 04 (arithmetic). Each curve flattens towards 1 ÷ (1 − α): past that, longer drafts only add draft cost. The playbooks use max_draft_len 5 (EAGLE-3), 4 (Draft-Target) and 3 (two-Spark Qwen3-235B).
